title: The Ivy Lee Method for Personal Productivity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A century-old productivity routine is recovered here as a still-serviceable discipline for leaders. The piece opens with a brief history of Ivy Ledbetter Lee, a pioneer of public relations and crisis communications who ran one of the first PR campaigns for the railroad industry and introduced the company news release and the internal employee magazine. That biographical setup is doing argumentative work: Lee is presented as a practitioner whose own output vouches for his method. The method itself is laid out in four steps — list the six most important tasks the night before, rank them by importance first thing in the morning, work them strictly in order, and roll anything unfinished onto tomorrow's six. The load-bearing rule, the author stresses, is the prohibition on starting the next task before the current one is fully complete, which is what converts a list into a sequence. The closing move is a challenge rather than a summary: the reader is asked whether they actually begin the day with the single most important thing, on the premise that some old ideas never lose their force.
points: The method's distinctive constraint is not the list of six but the refusal to begin task two until task one is finished, which is what blocks the drift into parallel half-work.
Ranking happens in the morning while the listing happens the night before, splitting the decision from the execution so the day opens with priorities already named.
Unfinished items are carried onto the next day's six rather than accumulating in a separate backlog, keeping the working list permanently capped.

The author leans on Lee's own record — first-ever PR campaigns, the news release, the internal morale magazine — as evidence that the method came from a genuinely productive practitioner rather than a theorist.
The implicit diagnosis is that most leaders never complete their most important task because they never attempt it first.
quotes: More than 100 years ago, Ivy Ledbetter Lee helped to pioneer the practice of Public Relations and Crisis Communications.
Lee was also the first to promote the idea of company news releases to the media and to favor internal magazines to increase employee morale inside large organizations.
He advised leaders to write down the six most important tasks for the next day before retiring for the evening.
Lee’s method then emphasized this critical point: Leaders should not begin the next task until they have fully completed the one before it.
The idea of prioritizing a short list of important tasks is baked into the psyche of just about everyone, thanks to Ivy Lee.
Do you start your day with the most important task and work hard to complete it before tackling anything else? Learn from Ivy Lee. Some great ideas never lose their impact.
